segments.title: The Fog and the System: Opening the Case

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of what many consider the greatest English novel of the nineteenth century.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we're going to open up Dickens' extraordinary machine — chapter by chapter, voice by voice, institution by institution.
Bleak House was published between 1852 and 1853, and it remains one of the most ambitious novels in any language — a work that begins, famously, in fog.
Not merely literal fog — though the fog is literal — but a fog that seems to seep from every institution Dickens describes.
To help us unpack all of that, I have three quite brilliant companions with me today.

First, Sir Edmund Leigh — a retired Oxford don whose lifelong engagement with Dickens has produced, among other things, a conviction that the novel's moral imagination matters far more than its political programme.
Edmund reads Esther Summerson as Dickens' true centre of gravity, and I suspect he'll have rather strong views about how we frame the fog.
Second, Professor James Blackstone — a legal historian who has spent his career studying Victorian institutions from the inside out.
James knows what the Court of Chancery actually was — not the caricature, but the grinding, fee-devouring reality — and that knowledge transforms how you read every page of this novel.
And third, Dr. Daniel Rosen — a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as an anatomy of class power.
Daniel's argument, and I find it genuinely compelling, is that Dickens was more radical than Dickens himself understood.
So — the fog.
The novel opens with one of the most extraordinary paragraphs in English prose, and I think we have to start there.
Edmund — you've read that opening more times than perhaps anyone alive.
One has read it a great many times, yes — and it has never once become familiar in the way that familiarity breeds indifference.
What Dickens does in that first chapter is something that had simply never been done before in English fiction.
He presents a world before he presents a story — a condition of existence, not a sequence of events.
The opening line sets the key immediately, and I think we should hear it.
"London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall. Implacable November weather."
Three noun phrases — no verb — and already the world is suspended, arrested, immovable.
The grammar itself enacts the paralysis that Chancery inflicts upon the living.
Now — I'll freely grant the fog is more than scenic decoration.
But I think those who rush too quickly to the systemic reading miss what is most astonishing: the sheer literary audacity of it.
I take Edmund's point about the literary audacity, and I wouldn't want to diminish it for a moment.
But the fog isn't merely a formal device — it has a specific address.
Dickens tells us exactly where it is thickest, and that precision is doing ideological work.
He writes — and this is the passage that arrested me the first time I read it —
"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping."
"And hard by Temple Bar, in Lincoln's Inn Hall, at the very heart of the fog, sits the Lord High Chancellor in his High Court of Chancery."
The fog flows everywhere — but it is densest at the seat of legal power.
That's not coincidence, and it's not just atmosphere — it is a structural argument written in weather.
What strikes me, coming at this as a legal historian rather than a literary critic, is quite how accurate that fog metaphor is as a description of how Chancery actually functioned.
The Court of Chancery in the 1850s was a genuine catastrophe — cases that had been running for decades, costs that devoured estates long before any judgment arrived.
Dickens wasn't exaggerating for comic or satirical effect — if anything, he was being conservative.
And this matters enormously for how we read the novel's famous opening claim — that Jarndyce and Jarndyce has become a cause so complicated that no man alive knows what it means.
Dickens puts it with wonderful deadpan precision —
"Jarndyce and Jarndyce drones on. This scarecrow of a suit has, in course of time, become so complicated that no man alive knows what it means."
A scarecrow of a suit — that is a precise image, not a fanciful one.
It frightens people away from the fields it was supposed to cultivate.
James, that is exactly the kind of historical grounding that redeems what might otherwise become merely sociological criticism.

One might add — following Dr. Johnson, who understood institutions rather better than most reformers — that the problem Dickens identifies is not the existence of the law but its corruption by time and complacency.
What the novel asks us to feel, in those opening pages, is a particular kind of moral revulsion — not class anger, but something closer to grief.
Grief that human arrangements, made with some original purpose of justice, have decayed into this.
Consider what Dickens says of the suitors themselves — those wretched people who have given their lives to the case —
"Innumerable children have been born into the cause; innumerable young people have married into it; innumerable old people have died out of it."
Born, married, died — the whole span of a human life consumed, and for nothing.
That is not a political indictment — it is an elegy.
An elegy — yes, beautifully put.
But elegies can be politically precise, and I'd argue Dickens is fully aware of who benefits from the fog.
The lawyers — Tulkinghorn, Vholes, even the ostensibly amiable Mr. Kenge — are all prospering magnificently while the fog persists.
Vholes is the figure I keep returning to — this gaunt, respectable, methodical devourer.
Dickens gives us a passage about him that is, I think, one of the most devastating satirical strokes in Victorian literature —
"Vholes is a very respectable man. He has not a large business, but he is a very respectable man. He is allowed by the greater attorneys... to be a most respectable man."
The word 'respectable' is deployed four times in a short passage — and each repetition drains it of meaning while loading it with menace.
This is Dickens showing us how ideological language works — how 'respectability' becomes a screen behind which the system feeds.
The Vholes passage is remarkable, and Daniel's right about the repetition — it's a technique Dickens uses with surgical intent.
But I'd add a piece of historical texture here, because the legal profession in the 1850s had a very specific structure that Dickens understood intimately.
Solicitors like Vholes were paid by the document — every letter written, every form filed, every delay engineered was another fee.
The incentive structure of Chancery literally rewarded the prolongation of suffering.
And Dickens captures this with the image of Vholes eating Richard Carstone — consuming him quietly, methodically, at the desk.
He writes — and this is almost unbearable in context —
"The name of Vholes... seems to start out of the firelight, to take a seat near Richard, to watch him, and to keep a wary eye upon that weakening morsel."
A morsel.
Richard Carstone — a young man with every advantage of birth and education — reduced to a morsel for a solicitor.
That word — morsel — is going to stay with me.
And I think what's already emerged, beautifully, in this conversation is a productive tension that will run through the whole series.
Edmund sees in Dickens' language an act of moral imagination — an elegy for wasted human lives.
Daniel sees a structural critique — a novelist who understood, perhaps better than he knew, how power reproduces itself through respectable fog.
And James is standing in the archive, telling us that the fog was real, the fees were real, and the bodies were real.
These readings, I suspect, are not as incompatible as they might appear.
In our next segment, we're going to move from the fog of Chancery to the fog of Chesney Wold — to Lady Dedlock, and to what Dickens does with the English aristocracy.
Do stay with us.

segments.title: Richard's Ambition: The Young Man's Trap

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time with the fog, with Chancery, with the slow grinding of the law.
Now I want to turn to what I think is the novel's most quietly devastating portrait — Richard Carstone.
Richard arrives in the novel as everything a young man should be — charming, handsome, generous, full of life.
And Dickens destroys him — not through villain, not through accident, but through a single sustained delusion.
With me today are Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Dr. Daniel Rosen.
Edmund, you've long argued that Richard is Dickens' most morally instructive young man. Where do we begin?
We begin, I think, with what Richard actually possesses — and what he chooses to squander.
Here is a young man with genuine gifts, a loving guardian in Jarndyce, the devotion of Ada Clare, and the friendship of Esther.
By every conventional measure, his foundations are sound.
And yet Dickens is merciless — because Richard cannot inhabit the present.
He is always looking toward the settlement of Jarndyce and Jarndyce as though it were a horizon that, once reached, would explain and justify everything.
Jarndyce himself puts it with terrible precision — and I think Dickens means us to hear a kind of prophecy in it.
'It's the one great principle of the English law to make business for itself.'
And Richard, poor Richard, has made that principle his own private cosmology.
I think Edmund is right to focus on the temporal dimension — the way Richard lives in a permanent, deferred future.
And as a legal historian I have to say — the Court of Chancery was specifically structured to produce exactly that effect.
Chancery suits in the nineteenth century could run for decades — fifty years was not unusual.
There was no mechanism for expedition, no incentive to settle — only the fee income of the court's own officers.
So when Dickens writes, and he does write it with surgical fury, that Chancery has its decaying houses and blighted lands in every shire — he is not exaggerating for effect.
He is describing a documented institutional pathology.
What happens to Richard is what Chancery was — structurally, systematically — designed to do to people like him.
And there's a class dimension here that I think we have to name.
Richard is a ward in Chancery — which means he is a young man whose claim to property is entirely mediated by the law.
He has no trade, no profession he can commit to — because the suit promises to render all that unnecessary.
He tries medicine, he tries the law, he tries the army — and Dickens is precise about this, each trial shorter and more erratic than the last.
The suit has colonised his imagination, and the result is that he cannot form what we might call a relationship to productive labour.
Esther captures it when she observes — and this is one of those moments where Dickens hides an indictment inside a gentle sentence —
'He had been educated in no habits of application and concentration.'
That word 'educated' is doing real work — this is not a failure of character alone, it is a failure of formation.
I want to push back gently on Daniel's framing — only gently, because much of it is persuasive.
But I am uneasy when the structural explanation entirely displaces the moral one.
Consider Esther Summerson — equally a ward, equally dependent on the court's resolution.
She does not succumb. She makes herself useful, minute by minute, in the actual world before her.
The contrast between Esther and Richard is, I believe, the moral engine of the novel.
Richard's tragedy is not simply that the system corrupted him.
It is that he chose — repeatedly, at each juncture — to let it.
That contrast with Esther is beautifully made — but I wonder whether Dickens lets Richard off rather less easily than Edmund suggests.
There is a moment — I think it is around chapter thirty-seven — where Woodcourt visits Richard and finds him in his lodgings near the court.
And Richard's situation is described in terms that are essentially pathological — a kind of legal addiction.
He has appointed Mr. Vholes as his solicitor, which tells you everything.
Vholes is one of the great comic-horrific creations of Victorian literature — a man who feeds on his clients with the measured patience of something reptilian.
Dickens gives Vholes this marvellous habit of removing his gloves finger by finger before speaking — the gesture of a man prepared to get his hands into something.
Richard could not have chosen a more perfect instrument of his own destruction.
Vholes — yes, and I think Dickens gives us the key to that character quite directly.
He tells us that Vholes is considered by the legal profession to be perfectly respectable.
And Dickens uses that respectability as a kind of acid.
He actually invites the reader to consider that if you put down Vholes, you must put down the whole system that produced and sustains him.
But on Richard and Edmund's question — I think they are both right and the tension between them is exactly the tension Dickens intends.
Dickens does not absolve Richard. Look at how Jarndyce puts it to him directly, with a sorrow that reads almost like a medical diagnosis:
'You have made a fatal mistake. Everything in this suit will only be made worse by going on.'
Richard hears it. He understands it. And he continues.
That is where the horror lives — not in ignorance but in the will's surrender to a seductive lie.
The will's surrender — that is very well put, and I will not quarrel with it.
What I find most moving — and Dickens makes it almost unbearable — is the way Richard's deterioration is registered through Ada's eyes.
Ada loves him without reservation, marries him secretly, and watches him consumed.
And near the end, Esther gives us this passage — and you must hear the quietness of it:
'He looked like a man who had fallen from a tower, and lay where he had fallen.'
Not murdered. Not betrayed by enemies. Fallen — as if gravity itself had finally finished its patient work on him.
That image of the fallen man carries such weight precisely because there is no villain to blame — only the long, slow erosion.
And I think that's what makes Richard so distinctly modern — we recognise that mode of self-undoing.
In our next segment, we'll follow the trail Richard himself could never leave behind — and look at what Chancery meant, in practice, for everyone else it consumed.

segments.title: Jo's Invisible Chains: Class, Disease, and Erasure

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're going deep into one of the novel's most devastating creations: Jo, the crossing-sweeper.
He is a boy who knows nothing, owns nothing, and is permitted to belong nowhere.
We're going to trace how Dickens uses Jo to expose class, disease, and what I'd call the Victorian art of erasure.
Edmund Leigh is with us — retired Oxford don, moral reader of Dickens, and the man most likely to quote Johnson before Jarndyce.
James Blackstone joins us as our legal historian — the person who can tell you exactly how broken Chancery was in practice, not just in fiction.
And Daniel Rosen is here as our cultural historian and the voice who refuses to let the system off the hook.
Edmund, let's begin with you — what is Jo, in the moral economy of this novel?
Jo is, I think, Dickens' most carefully constructed emblem of innocent suffering.
Not sentimental suffering — though one must concede Dickens is not above sentiment — but suffering that has been philosophically earned by the novel's architecture.
What strikes me always is the passage where Dickens steps back from the narrative altogether to address the reader directly.
He writes: "Jo lives — that is to say, Jo has not yet died — in a ruinous place known to the like of him by the name of Tom-all-Alone's."
That parenthetical — 'that is to say, Jo has not yet died' — is one of the most quietly annihilating phrases in all of English fiction.
To live is merely not yet to have died. That is the full extent of Jo's existence.
And Dickens puts it with such economy, such deliberate restraint, that the horror arrives before you've noticed it coming.
Edmund is absolutely right about the craft, but I want to press on what that craft is actually doing ideologically.
Jo does not merely suffer — he is made to move on.
Every constable, every beadle, every respectable citizen who encounters him delivers the same command: 'Move on.'
Dickens makes this into a refrain — almost a dark liturgy of exclusion.
He writes, with barely suppressed fury: "'Move on!' Jo is told. Jo moves on."
That repetition is not pathos — it's a structural argument.
The system does not need to kill Jo directly. It simply ensures he has no place in which to exist.
And the genius — if you want to call it that — is that every individual actor in this system believes they are merely doing their duty.
Daniel's point about duty hits hard when you place it in its actual legal context.
The Law of Settlement and Removal — still operative in Dickens' time — meant that a pauper could literally be moved on across parish boundaries as a matter of statute.
Jo isn't a metaphor for bureaucratic callousness. He is a precise documentary portrait of what that callousness looked like in action.
And when the inquest is held over Nemo's body, Jo is the only witness — a witness who, by law and by social consensus, cannot be believed.
Dickens makes that point with savage precision: the coroner dismisses Jo because he cannot take an oath, because he doesn't know what an oath is.
"Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on. Don't know that everybody has two names."
One name. One syllable. That is the entire archive of Jo's identity as far as the state is concerned.
James raises the inquest, and I think it's worth dwelling on what that scene achieves morally — not just institutionally.
Jo's ignorance is not presented as a defect of character. It is presented as a product of deliberate social abandonment.
Dickens is quite explicit about this in one of his most memorable rhetorical passages.
"It must be a strange state to be like Jo! To shuffle through the streets, unfamiliar with the shapes, and in utter darkness as to the meaning of those mysterious symbols."
The symbols are letters — writing itself.
Jo cannot read. Not because he lacks intelligence, but because no one has ever considered his intelligence worth cultivating.
That is an indictment of society, yes — but Dickens frames it as a moral indictment, not a merely political one.
And that distinction matters, I think, more than Dr. Rosen will allow.
I'll accept the distinction, Edmund, as long as we agree that the moral indictment has teeth only if it points somewhere.
And in this novel, it points very precisely at the institutions that reproduce Jo's condition generation after generation.
Consider what Dickens does with Tom-all-Alone's as a setting. It is not merely squalid — it is generative of squalor.
There's a passage in chapter sixteen — or thereabouts — that reads almost like a prophecy of contagion theory.
"There is not a drop of Tom's corrupted blood but propagates infection and contagion somewhere."
Disease here is not accidental. It is the logical output of a system that crams human beings into uninhabitable spaces and then is shocked — shocked — when illness spreads upward.
Jo carries smallpox — or a smallpox-like infection — to Esther Summerson. The bodies of the poor do not stay quarantined from the bodies of the comfortable.
Dickens understood this with a clarity that some of his philanthropic characters conspicuously lack.
The disease vector is historically fascinating, because smallpox and cholera were live debates in the 1850s.
John Snow's work on the Broad Street pump — mapping cholera to contaminated water — was published just two years after Bleak House.
Dickens was writing, in other words, at precisely the moment when miasma theory was collapsing under the weight of evidence.
And yet Tom-all-Alone's is still depicted in miasmatic terms — the very air is sick.
Which is more interesting than just correct science would have been, because it captures how contemporaries actually experienced urban poverty — as atmospheric, as inescapable.
And Jo himself is a carrier who doesn't know he's carrying. Which is the final cruelty — he is dangerous precisely because he has been denied the knowledge to protect anyone, including himself.
I want to return, if I may, to Jo's death — because I think it is the passage where Dickens earns everything he has spent.
It is a death scene of quite extraordinary restraint, which makes it all the more powerful.
Allan Woodcourt holds the dying boy and tries to lead him through the Lord's Prayer.
"'Hallowed be — thy —' Jo murmured it slowly, and when he had said it, looked most carefully at Woodcourt, to see whether he had done it right."
That single glance — 'to see whether he had done it right' — is unbearable.
All his life, Jo has been told he is wrong — that he is in the wrong place, says the wrong things, is the wrong kind of person.
And at the very moment of his death, his only desire is not comfort, not justice — but to have finally done something correctly.
Edmund, I won't argue with a word of that reading — it's right.
But directly after that moment, Dickens does something remarkable — he steps outside the narrative entirely.
He addresses the reader — addresses us — in his own voice, with undisguised fury.
"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, right reverends and wrong reverends of every order."
"Dead, men and women, born with heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around us every day."
That rolling anaphora — 'Dead, your Majesty... Dead, my lords...' — is not sentiment. It is an indictment of every class, every institution, every order of the established hierarchy.
And 'wrong reverends' — that phrase alone tells you Dickens is not simply grieving. He is assigning blame.
That passage was quoted in parliamentary debates about sanitary reform. Not immediately, but it entered the discourse.
Dickens corresponded with Edwin Chadwick — the great reformer of the Poor Law — and was acutely aware of the legislative battles over public health.
Jo is, in one sense, a composite portrait drawn from the reports Dickens had actually read — the Children's Employment Commission, the sanitary surveys.
But the documentary origin doesn't diminish the art — it deepens it. Because we know this boy existed, in his thousands.
And the novel's most quietly devastating insistence is that the system that produced Jo was entirely legal, entirely respectable, and entirely uninterested in its own consequences.
Dead, and dying thus around us every day — Dickens' words still land with extraordinary force.
Jo is invisible to the world of the novel, but Dickens makes him impossible for the reader to ignore — and that, I think, is the whole design.
In our next segment, we move to the fog — that opening image that haunts every room in the novel.
We'll be asking what it means, what it conceals, and whether it is — as Edmund suspects — a literary device, or something more systematic.

segments.title: Lady Dedlock's Double Life: Secrets and Scandal

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked — the podcast that takes Dickens' great fog-bound novel apart, chapter by chapter, thread by thread.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's most riveting creations: Lady Dedlock — aristocrat, secret-keeper, and, as Dickens arranges it, a woman whose past is a slow-burning fuse.
She presides over Chesney Wold with magnificent composure — and yet everything about her is a performance built over an abyss.
To help us read her, I'm delighted to have three exceptional minds with us.
Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don and our resident moral critic, who I suspect will find in Lady Dedlock a case study in the cost of self-deception.
Professor James Blackstone, legal historian, who will keep us honest about what scandal actually meant in the Victorian social and legal world.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen, who I imagine will argue that Lady Dedlock's secret is not merely personal — it is a structural exposure of the class that owns her.
Edmund, let's begin with first impressions — or rather, the impression Lady Dedlock is so carefully constructed to make.
She is introduced to us, of course, as the very image of aristocratic stasis — and that is quite deliberate.
Dickens establishes her in the early chapters at Chesney Wold as a woman who is bored — constitutionally, professionally, one might say terminally bored.
But Dickens is too great a novelist to let boredom be mere social affectation.
He tells us, with characteristic precision, that there is something in her face that Sir Leicester has never fathomed.
The phrase he uses is magnificent in its compression: her beauty is proud, and with its haughtiness, there is something frozen.
Frozen — there is the word that unlocks her entirely.
She has arrested herself, at great interior cost, in a posture that protects the secret — and that protects Sir Leicester from knowing who he has actually married.
The novel, from its very first pages, is asking us to understand that control of this magnitude is not superiority — it is terror, perfectly managed.
Edmund puts it beautifully, and I want to add a dimension that is easy to miss if one approaches her purely as a literary creation.
Lady Dedlock's situation, stripped of its fictional dressing, maps almost precisely onto the real legal and social circumstances of illegitimacy and female disgrace in the 1840s and 1850s.
She had a child — Esther — before marriage, by a man she loved, Captain Hawdon.
Had that become known, the consequences were not merely social embarrassment — they were, for a woman, essentially the end of every form of legitimate existence.
There was no divorce as we understand it, no readmission into respectable society, no second act.
And for Sir Leicester — a baronet with deep Tory roots, enormous pride in lineage — the disgrace would have been equally catastrophic, though of a different character.
Dickens understood this precisely, which is why Tulkinghorn is not merely a villain — he is a social mechanism.
He is the instrument by which the system enforces its terms on those who have stepped outside them.
James is right that Tulkinghorn is a mechanism — and that framing opens something up that I think is essential to reading this part of the novel.
Tulkinghorn doesn't want money from Lady Dedlock.
He wants power — specifically, the power that comes from knowing the secret of one of the highest women in England.
Dickens gives us the first crack in Lady Dedlock's composure in Chapter Two, when she sees Nemo's handwriting on a Chancery document and almost faints.
What strikes me is that Tulkinghorn notices — and says nothing in the moment, but files it away with the cold efficiency of a Victorian bureaucrat.
Dickens describes him with that famous image — the one portrait in the room, a painted allegory on the ceiling, whose pointing finger seems always to indicate Tulkinghorn below.
It is, he writes, Allegory, in Roman helmet and celestial linen, pointing at last in the direction of Tulkinghorn.
The class system points at its own lawyers — that is the image Dickens has quietly built.
And Lady Dedlock is caught in the sight-line of that finger from the moment we meet her.
I take Daniel's point about Tulkinghorn — and the allegorical ceiling is one of Dickens' great stage-sets.
But I want to return to Lady Dedlock herself, because I think the purely systemic reading risks flattening what is genuinely one of Dickens' most interior female characters.
There is a scene — and it is one I return to often — when she goes in secret to the churchyard where Hawdon is buried.
She is guided there by Jo — the crossing-sweeper — in a passage of extraordinary restraint and pathos.
She tells Jo, in that veiled, borrowed identity, that she is not a lady — she is only a servant.
And then Dickens gives us this: she put her hand upon her heart, and prayed in a quick, wild way, or almost swooned.
That is grief, not system.
That is a woman who has never been permitted to mourn — and who seizes, for one night, the right to do so in a pauper's graveyard.
I absolutely grant that — and I think Edmund puts the emotional truth of it exactly right.
But notice what makes that scene possible: she has to dress as a servant to visit the man she loved.
Her class is the very garment she must shed to feel anything authentic.
And she relies on Jo — a boy who himself has no name, no rights, no permanent place in the city — to lead her through it.
Dickens understood the irony: the highest woman in England guided by the lowest boy in London, through a system that will ultimately destroy them both.
And when Jo asks her what the grave is and she says, it is the gate into a better world, I don't read that as consolation.
I read it as a woman who has already decided she will not survive what is coming.
That reading of the churchyard scene is persuasive, and it connects to something I find historically remarkable about the novel's structure.
Dickens is careful — pointedly careful — about the question of who knows Lady Dedlock's secret, and when.
Tulkinghorn knows first, and he weaponises the knowledge methodically — never disclosing it, merely tightening the pressure.
What he is doing, in legal terms, is a form of coercion that Victorian law barely had language for.
The scene where he finally confronts her and tells her he has no immediate intention of acting — but that she is entirely in his hands — is as close to legalistic menace as Dickens ever wrote.
Dickens writes that she faced him with a face of great resolution, and with something of a proud anger in it.
That phrase — great resolution — matters enormously in context, because it is the one moment where her performance is not performance.
She is genuinely, defiantly herself — and the fact that it is immediately crushed is one of the novel's most quietly devastating turns.
James touches on something I think requires close attention: the question of Lady Dedlock's relationship to Esther.
There is, to my mind, no more delicate scene in all of Dickens than their recognition — when Esther first understands who Lady Dedlock is to her.
Lady Dedlock says to her, in a voice that Dickens renders in whispers almost on the page itself:
I am your wicked and unhappy mother. Oh, try to forgive me!
The word wicked is extraordinary there — because it is the vocabulary of self-condemnation, not of social ruin.
She is not asking forgiveness for the scandal — she is asking forgiveness for the abandonment.
That is a moral distinction that I think only a novelist of the first order would hold onto so firmly.
That scene is heartbreaking — and I want to honour that before I say anything else about it.
But I think what Dickens has also done — perhaps without fully knowing it — is to show us why the secret could never simply be confessed.
Lady Dedlock could not have come forward, could not have claimed Esther, because the entire social architecture they all inhabit would have collapsed on them both.
The secret is not a personal failure — it is a structural imprisonment.
And her death — discovered frozen at the gate of the pauper's burial ground in Nemo's clothes — is the novel's most savage structural punchline.
Dickens writes: the gate was barred; she lay against it.
She had tried, dressed as a servant, to return to the man the system had stolen from her — and the system's gate would not open.
That is not sentiment.
That image — the gate, the disguise, the body found by Esther who cannot yet believe what she is seeing — is one of the most fully achieved endings Dickens ever wrote for a major character.
And what strikes me, listening to the three of you, is that Lady Dedlock sustains all of these readings simultaneously — the moral, the historical, the structural.
Perhaps that is the mark of a great novel: it refuses to settle.
When we return, we'll be looking at the other secret at the heart of Bleak House — Chancery itself, and what Jarndyce and Jarndyce does to everyone it touches.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Bleak House and the Court of Chancery: Institutions of Decay

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the series in which we take one of the greatest novels in the English language apart — slowly, carefully, and with great relish.

I'm your host, and today we begin at the beginning — with fog, with Chancery, and with the question of what it means when the institutions that are supposed to sustain a society become the very thing that destroys it.
Joining me today are three scholars who between them bring the full weight of literary, legal, and political thinking to bear on this extraordinary novel.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don — a critic of the old school, for which I mean that as the highest possible compliment — who believes Dickens' genius is fundamentally moral rather than political.

Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who has spent his career studying the Victorian institutions that Dickens anatomised with such ferocity, and who can tell us what Chancery actually was.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as one of the most searching indictments of class power ever committed to the novel form.
Gentlemen, let's begin where Dickens begins — in the fog.
The opening of Bleak House is, I think, the finest sustained piece of prose Dickens ever wrote.
And one must read it aloud to feel the full force of it — the accumulation, the relentlessness.
He opens, as you say, with fog.
"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping."
That word — defiled — does everything.
The fog is not merely a meteorological fact; it is a moral condition — it corrupts what it touches, it reaches everywhere without discrimination.
Now, I am perfectly prepared to resist the reading that would make this fog simply a symbol of capitalism or institutional failure.
The fog is a literary device of enormous sophistication — it establishes the atmosphere in which character will be tested.
I take Edmund's point about the literary power — but I find I can't separate the fog from its destination, which is the Court of Chancery.
Dickens leads us through the fog and deposits us directly in the Lord Chancellor's court — and that is not an accident.
What people often don't realise is that the Court of Chancery in the eighteen-forties and fifties was genuinely one of the most dysfunctional legal institutions in the Western world.
Cases ran for decades — sometimes generations — because the court operated on a fee-per-filing system that made delay profitable for every officer of the court.
The case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce is a satire — but only barely.
There were real cases in Chancery that had consumed entire family estates by the time they were resolved — or simply abandoned.
Dickens himself says of Jarndyce and Jarndyce — and this is worth lingering on —
"that it has become so complicated that no man alive knows what it means; the parties to it understand it least."
That is not hyperbole — that is a precise description of how equity jurisdiction actually operated in cases of sufficient age and complexity.
James is right that Dickens is barely satirising — but I'd go further and say that the dysfunction is not a flaw in the system.
The dysfunction is the system working exactly as designed — it preserves wealth in suspension, out of reach of anyone who might actually need it.
And Dickens shows us this with a kind of controlled fury in the way he describes the suitors who have grown old waiting.
Miss Flite — this tiny, birdlike woman who appears in almost every court scene — she is the novel's most devastating image of what Chancery does to a human being over time.
She keeps caged birds she has named — and here Dickens is at his most brilliant, most deliberately allegorical —
Hope, Joy, Youth, Peace, Rest, Life, Dust, Ashes, Waste, Want, Ruin, Despair, Madness, Death, Cunning, Folly, Words, Wigs, Rags, Sheepskin, Plunder, Precedent, Jargon, Gammon, and Spinach.
That list moves from human aspiration to legal corruption to pure nihilism — and it does so in about thirty words.
That is Dickens knowing exactly what he is doing — and it is a political act, not merely a literary one.
I won't quarrel with the list of names — it is extraordinary — but I notice that Daniel reads it as a political act, and I read it as a moral one.
And I'm not sure the distinction is trivial.
Burke observed that when a man ceases to feel the force of moral obligation, no legal system can adequately substitute for it.
Chancery in Bleak House is not simply a class instrument — it is an institution that has lost its soul.
It was established in equity — in conscience — to do justice where the common law was too rigid to reach.
And Dickens understood that the tragedy of Chancery was precisely that perversion — a court of conscience that had become utterly unconscionable.
That is a moral catastrophe before it is a political one.
Edmund's point about equity jurisdiction is historically precise, and I'm glad he made it.
The Lord Chancellor's court was literally called a court of conscience — it was supposed to enforce trusts and moral obligations that common law courts couldn't touch.
The irony — the specific, surgical irony that Dickens deploys — is that this court of conscience has become the most conscienceless institution in England.
And Dickens makes this concrete through Gridley — the man from Shropshire — who appears early in the novel consumed by entirely legitimate rage.
Gridley says something that cuts to the heart of it — that he doesn't blame individual people in the court, not even the Lord Chancellor himself.
"I tell you it is the system. I accuse it. I tell you it has done this."
That is Dickens, through Gridley, making a structural argument — the evil is not personal, it is institutional.
And that distinction matters enormously — because institutional evil is far harder to prosecute, far easier to perpetuate.
The Gridley passage is one of the most important in the novel, and James has put his finger on exactly why.
But I want to connect it to something that Edmund and I do genuinely disagree about — which is what the systemic evil is in the service of.
Edmund sees moral decay — a court that has abandoned its founding conscience.
I see something more specific — I see a court that functions perfectly well for the lawyers, the Tulkinghorns, the Vholeses, who are paid by the hour and the page, regardless of outcome.
And Vholes — that magnificent monster — gives us a speech that is the novel's most nakedly ideological moment.
"The best of men, Mr. Carstone, the best of men are found wanting... I wish to say no more of any professional brother than that, and I say it with a full conviction of its truth."

And then there's the passage where Dickens describes how Vholes has a father to support in the Vale of Taunton and three daughters — and uses this to puncture every sentimental excuse made for predatory professionalism.
The system isn't broken — it is working precisely as the people who profit from it need it to work.
I find Vholes genuinely terrifying, and I don't think Daniel and I are as far apart on him as it might seem.
What makes Vholes so cold — so absolutely glacial as a character — is precisely that he has reduced all human relationship to professional transaction.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary image of him as vampiric — removing his black gloves, as though preparing to consume Richard.
My reading, however, is that this is a portrait of a man who has wilfully annihilated his own conscience — which is a moral failing first.
Dr. Johnson put it with his usual economy — "Hell is paved with good intentions" — and I sometimes think the novel's legal world is paved with professional ones.
That image of professional intentions as a kind of paving stone is one I suspect we'll return to.
What strikes me listening to the three of you is that you each agree the institution is catastrophically broken — you disagree about the nature of the break.
Edmund sees a failure of moral imagination; James sees a structural design that rewards delay; Daniel sees a system that serves capital at the expense of human life.
And perhaps what is most remarkable about Bleak House is that it accommodates all three readings simultaneously — because Dickens was a large enough novelist to be all three things at once.
In our next segment, we'll move deeper into the fog — to consider the human beings who are destroyed by this machinery, and what the novel asks us to feel about them.

segments.title: Narrative Fractured: How Dickens Tells His Story

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes one of the great Victorian novels apart — carefully, lovingly — to see how it works.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be spending a great deal of time inside a book that Dickens published in monthly parts between 1852 and 1853.
A book about a lawsuit that never ends, a heroine who barely believes in her own existence, and a fog so thick you can taste it.
Today we're starting with something fundamental: how Dickens actually tells this story — because the answer is stranger and more radical than most readers expect.
To help us, I'm delighted to introduce three guests who bring genuinely different lenses to this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose great argument is that Bleak House is, above all else, a novel about character — about what people do when institutions fail them.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who has spent a career mapping the real machinery behind Dickens' fictions — the actual courts, the actual poor, the actual stakes.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as a systematic anatomy of class power — and who will argue, I suspect, that Dickens understood more than he admitted.
Let us begin with the most obvious and most disorienting fact about this novel: it has two narrators.
The double narration is, I think, the formal decision that makes Bleak House what it is — and it is a decision that has never quite been replicated with equal success.
Dickens gives us, on the one hand, the unnamed third-person narrator — present tense, omniscient, implacable — the great prosecuting voice of the novel.
And on the other hand, Esther Summerson — first person, past tense, modest to the point of self-erasure — who writes her own portion of the story years after the events it describes.
The contrast is almost shocking when you feel it for the first time.

The third-person narrator opens the novel with that extraordinary assault on the senses — the fog, the mud, the court — and does so in the present tense, as though history itself were still happening.
"London. Michaelmas Term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall. Implacable November weather."
Three noun phrases, no verbs — the grammar itself refusing to move forward, to progress, to resolve.
That is Dickens announcing, in the first four words of his novel, exactly what Chancery does to time.
Edmund's point about the present tense is one I find genuinely illuminating from a legal-historical angle.
Chancery cases in the mid-nineteenth century were not ancient history — they were living, ongoing catastrophes.
The real case of Jennens v. Jennens, which scholars have long considered a partial model for Jarndyce and Jarndyce, ran from 1798 well into the 1870s.
So when the third-person narrator speaks in the present tense, he is not being stylistically adventurous — he is being accurate.
What I find equally interesting is what the double narration does to the question of knowledge — of who can know what, and when.
The third-person narrator sees everything and yet is curiously powerless — he can describe Lady Dedlock's secret, Jo's death, Tulkinghorn's murder, but he cannot intervene.
Esther, by contrast, is embedded in events — she acts, she nurses, she loves, she is disfigured by smallpox — but she writes from retrospect, from safety, from survival.
Between the two of them, you get the full range of what it means to live inside history rather than merely observe it.
Both of those framings are important, but I want to push on something that I think gets underplayed — which is the ideological work the double narration performs.

The third-person narrator has a quality that I'd call systemic vision — he sees the fog, the slums, the court, the philanthropic societies, the great houses — all as parts of a single, connected apparatus of social reproduction.
Esther, on the other hand, can only see what her position allows her to see — the domestic, the personal, the immediate.
And that is not a criticism of Esther — it is a description of how class and gender circumscribe perception.
Look at what happens in Chapter Three, when Esther first encounters Chancery — she describes it through the filter of personal anxiety, of not knowing who she is or why she's there.
She writes: "I had never heard of Jarndyce and Jarndyce — which has been moving on for I don't know how many years."
She doesn't know how many years — and that ignorance is structural, not personal.
The system is designed to be opaque to those it devours — and the novel's formal split enacts that opacity beautifully.
I take Daniel's point about structural opacity, though I would frame the same observation rather differently.
What strikes me about Esther's narration is not primarily her limitation but her grace — the extraordinary quality of attention she brings to those around her.
She is the novel's moral instrument precisely because she sees people rather than systems.
There is a moment in her narration — I believe it is in the chapters following her illness — where she describes her own face in the mirror after the smallpox.
She writes: "I was very much changed — I knew that; I had undergone great suffering, great fatigue; and I had been very ill."
And yet she moves immediately to concern for those nursing her — for Charley, for Ada — with barely a pause for self-pity.
That is not a character constrained by her position — that is a character who has chosen her moral orientation, and chosen it at considerable cost.
I want to come back to the formal mechanics for a moment, because I think there is a dimension that neither Edmund nor Daniel has quite touched on yet.
Bleak House was published in monthly parts — nineteen monthly numbers, the last being a double number.
That means Dickens was managing the two narrative streams simultaneously, in real time, in front of an audience that was reading and discussing and speculating month by month.
The interleaving of the two narrators is therefore not only a literary strategy — it is a serialisation strategy.
The third-person chapters give you breadth and menace — Lady Dedlock glimpsed at the window, Tulkinghorn circling, the fog always thickening.
Esther's chapters give you warmth, forward momentum, the pleasure of being with someone you trust.
Dickens understood, as any good serial editor understands, that you must give your reader a place to breathe — and Esther is that place.
James is absolutely right about the serial logic, and it raises something I find compelling about the way the two narrative registers actually contaminate each other.
There are moments — and they are some of the most unsettling in the novel — where the boundary between the two narratives becomes unstable.
Consider the death of Jo — which arrives in the third-person narrative, in one of the novel's most famous passages.

"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order. Dead, men and women, born with Heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around us every day."
That is the prosecutorial narrator at his most unguarded — directly addressing the reader, abandoning the pretence of detached observation.
But what makes it so powerful is that we have already experienced Jo through Esther's eyes — through her warmth, her tangible distress at his suffering.
The two streams have built a single grief — systemic and personal, public and private — that neither voice could have achieved alone.
That passage about Jo is, I will concede, one of those moments where Dickens simply overwhelms one's critical defences.
One has reservations about Dickens' rhetoric — its occasional excess, its manipulation of sentiment — and then one reads "Dead, your Majesty" and one's reservations quietly retire.
But I want to add something to what Daniel said about contamination between the two voices.
There is a formal mystery at the heart of Esther's narration that Dickens never fully resolves — which is: who is she writing for?
She says at the outset that she has been asked to set down her portion of the story — but by whom, and to what end, we are never precisely told.
Her narration thus floats in a curious space — intimate as a diary, yet addressed to an unspecified reader.
It is the novel's most persistent formal puzzle, and I rather think Dickens left it deliberately open — because Esther's uncertainty about her audience mirrors her uncertainty about her own identity.
That question of address is one that legal historians find rather resonant, as it happens.
Documents in Chancery — petitions, bills of complaint, answers — were also written to an unspecified but theoretically omniscient authority.
The Lord Chancellor, in theory, stood in loco parentis to wards of court — and Esther, of course, is literally a ward in Chancery.
So there is a very dark possible reading of her narration — that she is, unconsciously, addressing her testimony to the very institution that has governed her life from birth.
Writing to a court that cannot hear her — that is both her formal situation and, in miniature, the situation of everyone in this novel.
That is a devastating observation, James, and I think it points to something Dickens understood at a level just below conscious intention.
The novel's fractured form — two voices, two tenses, two epistemological positions — is not a technical novelty.
It is a formal argument about the impossibility of unified perspective in a society divided against itself.
No single narrator can tell this story coherently — because no single subject position in Victorian England could encompass both Chesney Wold and Tom-all-Alone's.
Dickens had to split the narration because the society itself was split — and he was honest enough, formally, to acknowledge that.
I think that is an extraordinary place to pause — the form of the novel as an argument the novelist may not have known he was making.
Edmund, James, Daniel — thank you.
We've been thinking about narrative structure — the two voices, the two tenses, the formal logic of the split — and what that tells us about the world Dickens was trying to see whole.
In our next segment, we'll descend from the structural to the granular — and look at what this novel does with its fog: literal, metaphorical, and something in between.

segments.title: Fog Lifts: Ruin, Redemption, and What Remains

utterances.text: We've spent this episode deep in Dickens' fog — in the courts, the tenements, the great houses falling to ruin.
Now, in our closing segment, we ask the hardest question the novel poses: does the fog ever lift?
What remains when Chancery is done with its victims, when the estate is exhausted, when Jo has moved on?
Edmund, I want to start with you on this — because I think your reading of the novel is ultimately about what survives.
The fog lifts, but only for those who have earned, in some moral sense, the right to see clearly.
Dickens is quite precise about this — and it's a precision his more impatient critics overlook.
Esther ends the novel in a second Bleak House — a home rebuilt, a family made real — and Dickens gives her a passage of almost startling simplicity.
"I have a houseful of the happiest children in the world... and I have an old Dame Durden smile to spare for all of them."
That is not irony. That is not Dickens hedging his bets.
It is the reward that virtue earns in a world where virtue is genuinely difficult — and Esther has been tested at every turn.
I want to sit with that image for a moment before we move to celebration, because it's a complicated one.
Esther's second Bleak House is built in Yorkshire — at a remove from the wreckage of Chancery, from Tom-All-Alone's, from everything the first half of the novel showed us.
And that distance is purchased — paid for, in part, by Jarndyce's extraordinary act of self-abnegation.
Jo gets no second Bleak House. Jo gets the churchyard.
And Dickens knows this — which is why the direct address at Jo's death is one of the most politically charged passages he ever wrote.
"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order."
That accumulation — the deliberate, hammering repetition — is Dickens pointing his finger at the very people holding the book.
The Jo passage is the one that historians keep returning to — because it isn't sentiment, whatever people say.
Dickens had the figures. He knew the mortality rates in the St. Giles rookeries, he knew what the crossing-sweepers' lives actually cost.
When he writes that Jo is "not one of Mrs. Jellyby's objects of charity" — that line lands differently when you know it's also a legal category.
Jo cannot be admitted to a parish, cannot claim poor relief, cannot be buried with a name that anyone official will record.
Dickens understood that the fog in this novel is not merely atmospheric — it is administrative.
I take James's point entirely — and I don't wish to soften it.
But I would insist that what redeems the novel is not that the system is reformed — it isn't, and Dickens knows it isn't.
What redeems it is Esther Summerson herself — this illegitimate, unwanted child who becomes the moral centre of an enormous and chaotic world.
Her narrative is an act of recovery — of making sense of experience through the discipline of narration itself.
Consider what she says near the close — almost embarrassed by her own happiness, still that self-deprecating voice:
"I am not clever. I don't know how it is; I seem to be always writing about myself."
That modesty is itself a kind of heroism — and Dickens earns every bit of her happiness by making us feel how hard it was to arrive there.
The double narrative is what makes this novel so endlessly arguable — and I mean that as the highest praise.
Esther narrates in the past tense — she has survived, she knows the shape of the story. The third-person narrator speaks only in the present.
And that present tense is relentless — "it is" and "there is" and "the fog rolls in" — because that world doesn't end.
Esther gets her redemption arc. Tom-All-Alone's does not.
And Dickens is honest enough — or radical enough, perhaps, without quite knowing it — to hold both truths simultaneously.
The Jarndyce will exhausting itself is worth lingering on as a closing image — because it's the one moment where the institutional machinery actually stops.
Not because justice is done. The costs have simply consumed the entire estate.
Dickens had researched real Chancery cases — Jennens v Jennens ran for over a century and ended in precisely this way.
The system doesn't reform. It simply runs out of things to eat.
And Dickens gives us Richard Carstone — brilliant, ruined Richard — as the emblem of what that appetite costs in human terms.
"The clouds have cleared from you and you are at peace" — Ada says to him at the end, and it's true, in the most terrible way.
Death is the only exit Chancery grants without a fee.
That line of James's will stay with me. Death is the only exit Chancery grants without a fee.
And yet Dickens also gives us Inspector Bucket — this extraordinary figure who actually solves things.
Bucket finds Lady Dedlock. He is too late, but he finds her.
And where does he find her? At the gate of the pauper's cemetery — the place where her connection to Jo, to the whole suppressed underclass of the novel, comes full circle.
Dickens was incapable, in the end, of fully separating the fates of the high and the low. And that is his most profound instinct as a novelist.
Lady Dedlock at that gate — I think that scene is the emotional and structural heart of the whole novel.
She has crossed from Chesney Wold to Tom-All-Alone's. She has put on the clothes of Jenny, the brickmaker's wife.
The aristocracy literally dressing itself in the rags of the poor — as a disguise, yes, but also as a penance.
And Esther, finding her mother there, describes her — and this is one of Dickens' great sentences —
"the mother of the dead child" — I move and cry and reach out — and she is cold, she is gone.
The fog doesn't lift for Lady Dedlock. She is the fog — the secrecy and shame and social performance that the whole ruling class requires.
I want to ask each of you, as we close — if you had to name what remains when the fog finally clears, what is Dickens' answer?
Edmund — briefly — what survives?
Character survives. The goodness that Esther has tended in herself, against every pressure — that survives.
Burke called it the partnership between the living, the dead, and those yet to be born.
Esther's second Bleak House is exactly that — a new generation inheriting something worth having, despite everything Chancery has done.
The question remains. That's what survives.
Dickens doesn't resolve the poverty, the institutional cruelty, the fog over Tom-All-Alone's.
He hands it to the reader — this burning, specific, documented indictment — and he says: now you carry it.
Jo survives — as an indictment that cannot be buried however deep you dig.
Dickens ends his great attack on Chancery not with a verdict but with a valediction — and the valediction belongs to the crossing-sweeper.
"Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order. Dead, men and women, born with heavenly compassion in your hearts."
And then: "And dying thus around us every day."
Every day. That is what remains. That is the fog that doesn't lift.
Edmund Leigh, James Blackstone, Daniel Rosen — it has been a genuine pleasure to think through this great novel with you.
Bleak House is one of those works that refuses to be finished with — it keeps reading us back, as Dickens always does.
Thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.
We'll meet you in the fog.

London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.

Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and
meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers
of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.
Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights. Fog creeping
into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and
hovering in the rigging of great ships; fog drooping on the gunwales
of barges and small boats. Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient
Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog
in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper,
down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of
his shivering little ’prentice boy on deck. Chance people on the
bridges peeping over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog
all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the
misty clouds.

Jarndyce and Jarndyce drones on. This scarecrow of a suit has, in
course of time, become so complicated that no man alive knows what it
means. The parties to it understand it least, but it has been
observed that no two Chancery lawyers can talk about it for five
minutes without coming to a total disagreement as to all the
premises. Innumerable children have been born into the cause;
innumerable young people have married into it; innumerable old people
have died out of it. Scores of persons have deliriously found
themselves made parties in Jarndyce and Jarndyce without knowing how
or why; whole families have inherited legendary hatreds with the
suit. The little plaintiff or defendant who was promised a new
rocking-horse when Jarndyce and Jarndyce should be settled has grown
up, possessed himself of a real horse, and trotted away into the
other world. Fair wards of court have faded into mothers and
grandmothers; a long procession of Chancellors has come in and gone
out; the legion of bills in the suit have been transformed into mere
bills of mortality; there are not three Jarndyces left upon the earth
perhaps since old Tom Jarndyce in despair blew his brains out at a
coffee-house in Chancery Lane; but Jarndyce and Jarndyce still drags
its dreary length before the court, perennially hopeless.

It was a question much discussed between him and my guardian what
arrangements should be made for his living in London while he
experimented on the law, for we had long since gone back to Bleak
House, and it was too far off to admit of his coming there oftener
than once a week. My guardian told me that if Richard were to settle
down at Mr. Kenge’s he would take some apartments or chambers where
we too could occasionally stay for a few days at a time; “but, little
woman,” he added, rubbing his head very significantly, “he hasn’t
settled down there yet!” The discussions ended in our hiring for him,
by the month, a neat little furnished lodging in a quiet old house
near Queen Square. He immediately began to spend all the money he had

The one great principle of the English law is to make business for
itself. There is no other principle distinctly, certainly, and
consistently maintained through all its narrow turnings. Viewed by
this light it becomes a coherent scheme and not the monstrous maze
the laity are apt to think it. Let them but once clearly perceive

Mr. Skimpole was as agreeable at breakfast as he had been overnight.
There was honey on the table, and it led him into a discourse about
bees. He had no objection to honey, he said (and I should think he
had not, for he seemed to like it), but he protested against the
overweening assumptions of bees. He didn’t at all see why the busy
bee should be proposed as a model to him; he supposed the bee liked
to make honey, or he wouldn’t do it—nobody asked him. It was not
necessary for the bee to make such a merit of his tastes. If every
confectioner went buzzing about the world banging against everything
that came in his way and egotistically calling upon everybody to take
notice that he was going to his work and must not be interrupted, the
world would be quite an unsupportable place. Then, after all, it was
a ridiculous position to be smoked out of your fortune with brimstone
as soon as you had made it. You would have a very mean opinion of a
Manchester man if he spun cotton for no other purpose. He must say he
thought a drone the embodiment of a pleasanter and wiser idea. The
drone said unaffectedly, “You will excuse me; I really cannot attend
to the shop! I find myself in a world in which there is so much to
see and so short a time to see it in that I must take the liberty of
looking about me and begging to be provided for by somebody who
doesn’t want to look about him.” This appeared to Mr. Skimpole to be
the drone philosophy, and he thought it a very good philosophy,
always supposing the drone to be willing to be on good terms with the
bee, which, so far as he knew, the easy fellow always was, if the
consequential creature would only let him, and not be so conceited
about his honey!

In the neighbouring court, where the Lord Chancellor of the rag and
bottle shop dwells, there is a general tendency towards beer and
supper. Mrs. Piper and Mrs. Perkins, whose respective sons, engaged
with a circle of acquaintance in the game of hide and seek, have been
lying in ambush about the by-ways of Chancery Lane for some hours and
scouring the plain of the same thoroughfare to the confusion of
passengers—Mrs. Piper and Mrs. Perkins have but now exchanged
congratulations on the children being abed, and they still linger on
a door-step over a few parting words. Mr. Krook and his lodger, and
the fact of Mr. Krook’s being “continually in liquor,” and the
testamentary prospects of the young man are, as usual, the staple of
their conversation. But they have something to say, likewise, of the
Harmonic Meeting at the Sol’s Arms, where the sound of the piano
through the partly opened windows jingles out into the court, and
where Little Swills, after keeping the lovers of harmony in a roar
like a very Yorick, may now be heard taking the gruff line in a
concerted piece and sentimentally adjuring his friends and patrons to
“Listen, listen, listen, tew the wa-ter fall!” Mrs. Perkins and Mrs.
Piper compare opinions on the subject of the young lady of
professional celebrity who assists at the Harmonic Meetings and who
has a space to herself in the manuscript announcement in the window,
Mrs. Perkins possessing information that she has been married a year
and a half, though announced as Miss M. Melvilleson, the noted siren,
and that her baby is clandestinely conveyed to the Sol’s Arms every
night to receive its natural nourishment during the entertainments.
“Sooner than which, myself,” says Mrs. Perkins, “I would get my
living by selling lucifers.” Mrs. Piper, as in duty bound, is of the
same opinion, holding that a private station is better than public
applause, and thanking heaven for her own (and, by implication, Mrs.
Perkins’) respectability. By this time the pot-boy of the Sol’s Arms
appearing with her supper-pint well frothed, Mrs. Piper accepts that
tankard and retires indoors, first giving a fair good night to Mrs.
Perkins, who has had her own pint in her hand ever since it was
fetched from the same hostelry by young Perkins before he was sent to
bed. Now there is a sound of putting up shop-shutters in the court
and a smell as of the smoking of pipes; and shooting stars are seen
in upper windows, further indicating retirement to rest. Now, too,
the policeman begins to push at doors; to try fastenings; to be
suspicious of bundles; and to administer his beat, on the hypothesis
that every one is either robbing or being robbed.

Jo lives—that is to say, Jo has not yet died—in a ruinous place
known to the like of him by the name of Tom-all-Alone’s. It is a

crazy houses were seized upon, when their decay was far advanced, by

evil in its every footprint than Lord Coodle, and Sir Thomas Doodle,

to do it.

c16:p11.text:
It must be a strange state to be like Jo! To shuffle through the
streets, unfamiliar with the shapes, and in utter darkness as to the
meaning, of those mysterious symbols, so abundant over the shops, and
at the corners of streets, and on the doors, and in the windows! To
see people read, and to see people write, and to see the postmen
deliver letters, and not to have the least idea of all that
language—to be, to every scrap of it, stone blind and dumb! It must
be very puzzling to see the good company going to the churches on
Sundays, with their books in their hands, and to think (for perhaps
Jo DOES think at odd times) what does it all mean, and if it means
anything to anybody, how comes it that it means nothing to me? To be
hustled, and jostled, and moved on; and really to feel that it would
appear to be perfectly true that I have no business here, or there,
or anywhere; and yet to be perplexed by the consideration that I AM
here somehow, too, and everybody overlooked me until I became the
creature that I am! It must be a strange state, not merely to be told
that I am scarcely human (as in the case of my offering myself for a
witness), but to feel it of my own knowledge all my life! To see the
horses, dogs, and cattle go by me and to know that in ignorance I
belong to them and not to the superior beings in my shape, whose
delicacy I offend! Jo’s ideas of a criminal trial, or a judge, or a
bishop, or a government, or that inestimable jewel to him (if he only
knew it) the Constitution, should be strange! His whole material and
immaterial life is wonderfully strange; his death, the strangest
thing of all.
c16:p11.summary: The narrator powerfully explores Jo's alienation from literate society, meaning-making, and human dignity, showing how systemic exclusion has made him feel less than human.

Upon that, Mr. Skimpole began to talk, for the first time since our
arrival, in his usual gay strain. He said, Well, it was really very
pleasant to see how things lazily adapted themselves to purposes.
Here was this Mr. Gridley, a man of a robust will and surprising
energy—intellectually speaking, a sort of inharmonious
blacksmith—and he could easily imagine that there Gridley was, years
ago, wandering about in life for something to expend his superfluous
combativeness upon—a sort of Young Love among the thorns—when the
Court of Chancery came in his way and accommodated him with the exact
thing he wanted. There they were, matched, ever afterwards! Otherwise
he might have been a great general, blowing up all sorts of towns, or
he might have been a great politician, dealing in all sorts of
parliamentary rhetoric; but as it was, he and the Court of Chancery
had fallen upon each other in the pleasantest way, and nobody was
much the worse, and Gridley was, so to speak, from that hour provided
for. Then look at Coavinses! How delightfully poor Coavinses (father
of these charming children) illustrated the same principle! He, Mr.
Skimpole, himself, had sometimes repined at the existence of
Coavinses. He had found Coavinses in his way. He could had dispensed
with Coavinses. There had been times when, if he had been a sultan,
and his grand vizier had said one morning, “What does the Commander
of the Faithful require at the hands of his slave?” he might have
even gone so far as to reply, “The head of Coavinses!” But what
turned out to be the case? That, all that time, he had been giving
employment to a most deserving man, that he had been a benefactor to
Coavinses, that he had actually been enabling Coavinses to bring up
these charming children in this agreeable way, developing these
social virtues! Insomuch that his heart had just now swelled and the
tears had come into his eyes when he had looked round the room and
thought, “I was the great patron of Coavinses, and his little
comforts were MY work!”

came into our place one morning after breakfast, and finding my
little woman (which I name Mrs. Snagsby when I use that appellation)

moving heaven and earth (including, of course, the Chancellor) after
Michaelmas term; and when I ultimately congratulate you, sir,” says
Mr. Vholes with the severity of a determined man, “when I ultimately
congratulate you, sir, with all my heart, on your accession to
fortune—which, but that I never give hopes, I might say something
further about—you will owe me nothing beyond whatever little balance
may be then outstanding of the costs as between solicitor and client
not included in the taxed costs allowed out of the estate. I pretend
to no claim upon you, Mr. C., but for the zealous and active
discharge—not the languid and routine discharge, sir: that much
credit I stipulate for—of my professional duty. My duty prosperously
ended, all between us is ended.”

Charley and I had reason to call it the most friendly of villages, I
am sure, for in a week’s time the people were so glad to see us go
by, though ever so frequently in the course of a day, that there were
faces of greeting in every cottage. I had known many of the grown
people before and almost all the children, but now the very steeple
began to wear a familiar and affectionate look. Among my new friends
was an old old woman who lived in such a little thatched and
whitewashed dwelling that when the outside shutter was turned up on
its hinges, it shut up the whole house-front. This old lady had a
grandson who was a sailor, and I wrote a letter to him for her and
drew at the top of it the chimney-corner in which she had brought him
up and where his old stool yet occupied its old place. This was
considered by the whole village the most wonderful achievement in the
world, but when an answer came back all the way from Plymouth, in
which he mentioned that he was going to take the picture all the way
to America, and from America would write again, I got all the credit
that ought to have been given to the post-office and was invested
with the merit of the whole system.

c48:p128.text:
A very quiet night. When the moon shines very brilliantly, a solitude
and stillness seem to proceed from her that influence even crowded
places full of life. Not only is it a still night on dusty high roads
and on hill-summits, whence a wide expanse of country may be seen in
repose, quieter and quieter as it spreads away into a fringe of trees
against the sky with the grey ghost of a bloom upon them; not only is
it a still night in gardens and in woods, and on the river where the
water-meadows are fresh and green, and the stream sparkles on among
pleasant islands, murmuring weirs, and whispering rushes; not only
does the stillness attend it as it flows where houses cluster thick,
where many bridges are reflected in it, where wharves and shipping
make it black and awful, where it winds from these disfigurements
through marshes whose grim beacons stand like skeletons washed
ashore, where it expands through the bolder region of rising grounds,
rich in cornfield wind-mill and steeple, and where it mingles with
the ever-heaving sea; not only is it a still night on the deep, and
on the shore where the watcher stands to see the ship with her spread
wings cross the path of light that appears to be presented to only
him; but even on this stranger’s wilderness of London there is some
rest. Its steeples and towers and its one great dome grow more
ethereal; its smoky house-tops lose their grossness in the pale
effulgence; the noises that arise from the streets are fewer and are
softened, and the footsteps on the pavements pass more tranquilly
away. In these fields of Mr. Tulkinghorn’s inhabiting, where the
shepherds play on Chancery pipes that have no stop, and keep their
sheep in the fold by hook and by crook until they have shorn them
exceeding close, every noise is merged, this moonlight night, into a
distant ringing hum, as if the city were a vast glass, vibrating.
c48:p128.summary: The narrator provides an extended, elaborate description of moonlit calm across the natural world, from countryside to ocean, ending with Chancery metaphors for Tulkinghorn's world.
c48:p128.best_quote: In these fields of Mr. Tulkinghorn's inhabiting, where the shepherds play on Chancery pipes that have no stop, and keep their sheep in the fold by hook and by crook until they have shorn them exceeding close, every noise is merged, this moonlight night, into a distant ringing hum, as if the city were a vast glass, vibrating.

“The captain in the army being dead, she believed herself safe; but a
train of circumstances with which I need not trouble you led to
discovery. As I received the story, they began in an imprudence on
her own part one day when she was taken by surprise, which shows how
difficult it is for the firmest of us (she was very firm) to be
always guarded. There was great domestic trouble and amazement, you
may suppose; I leave you to imagine, Sir Leicester, the husband’s
grief. But that is not the present point. When Mr. Rouncewell’s
townsman heard of the disclosure, he no more allowed the girl to be
patronized and honoured than he would have suffered her to be trodden
underfoot before his eyes. Such was his pride, that he indignantly
took her away, as if from reproach and disgrace. He had no sense of
the honour done him and his daughter by the lady’s condescension; not
the least. He resented the girl’s position, as if the lady had been
the commonest of commoners. That is the story. I hope Lady Dedlock
will excuse its painful nature.”

“The number, sir,” said Mr. Vholes parenthetically, “I believe I have
already mentioned. If Mr. C. is to continue to play for this
considerable stake, sir, he must have funds. Understand me! There are
funds in hand at present. I ask for nothing; there are funds in hand.
But for the onward play, more funds must be provided, unless Mr. C.
is to throw away what he has already ventured, which is wholly and
solely a point for his consideration. This, sir, I take the
opportunity of stating openly to you as the friend of Mr. C. Without
funds I shall always be happy to appear and act for Mr. C. to the
extent of all such costs as are safe to be allowed out of the estate,
not beyond that. I could not go beyond that, sir, without wronging
some one. I must either wrong my three dear girls or my venerable
father, who is entirely dependent on me, in the Vale of Taunton; or
some one. Whereas, sir, my resolution is (call it weakness or folly

cP:p2.text:
But as it is wholesome that the parsimonious public should know what
has been doing, and still is doing, in this connexion, I mention here
that everything set forth in these pages concerning the Court of
Chancery is substantially true, and within the truth. The case of
Gridley is in no essential altered from one of actual occurrence,
made public by a disinterested person who was professionally
acquainted with the whole of the monstrous wrong from beginning to
end. At the present moment (August, 1853) there is a suit before the
court which was commenced nearly twenty years ago, in which from
thirty to forty counsel have been known to appear at one time, in
which costs have been incurred to the amount of seventy thousand
pounds, which is A FRIENDLY SUIT, and which is (I am assured) no
nearer to its termination now than when it was begun. There is
another well-known suit in Chancery, not yet decided, which was
commenced before the close of the last century and in which more than
double the amount of seventy thousand pounds has been swallowed up in
costs. If I wanted other authorities for Jarndyce and Jarndyce, I
could rain them on these pages, to the shame of—a parsimonious
public.
cP:p2.summary: Dickens asserts the factual basis of his Chancery depictions by citing real cases: a twenty-year suit with seventy thousand pounds in costs and another century-old suit with double that amount.
cP:p2.best_quote: If I wanted other authorities for Jarndyce and Jarndyce, I could rain them on these pages, to the shame of—a parsimonious public.

your pardon. I am not polite, I know. I beg your pardon! Sir,” with
